name: Warehouses and Lakehouses for AI
title: Warehouses and Lakehouses for AI
answer: A data warehouse holds structured, cleaned analytical tables that people query with SQL, while a lakehouse keeps raw files in open formats and layers table semantics and SQL over them so the same storage serves both reporting and machine learning. The two have converged in practice: the major platforms now offer AI functions and model serving inside the platform, so data does not have to leave governed storage to be used by a model. For a working professional this means the warehouse or lakehouse is no longer only a reporting endpoint, it is also a place where features are assembled, models are trained or called, and predictions are written back as ordinary tables. The scope of the topic is therefore the storage and query layer that sits underneath most enterprise AI work, not the modelling techniques themselves.

sections.body: A data warehouse holds structured, cleaned analytical tables that people query with SQL, while a lakehouse keeps raw files in open formats and layers table semantics and SQL over them so the same storage serves both reporting and machine learning. The two have converged in practice: the major platforms now offer AI functions and model serving inside the platform, so data does not have to leave governed storage to be used by a model. For a working professional this means the warehouse or lakehouse is no longer only a reporting endpoint, it is also a place where features are assembled, models are trained or called, and predictions are written back as ordinary tables. The scope of the topic is therefore the storage and query layer that sits underneath most enterprise AI work, not the modelling techniques themselves.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Underneath, these systems rest on object storage for the bulk of the data, a metadata and catalog layer that tracks tables, schemas, permissions and file locations, and a distributed compute engine that parses SQL and executes it across many machines. Warehouses traditionally coupled storage and compute tightly, while lakehouses separate them so each can be scaled or paused independently, and open table formats provide the transaction log that makes files behave like tables. Query engines read columnar files, push filters down to skip irrelevant data, and cache hot results, which is what keeps interactive SQL responsive over very large datasets. Model serving inside the platform typically runs on the same cluster or a managed endpoint beside it, so inference reads features directly from governed tables rather than through a separate copy.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The daily work is mostly SQL plus orchestration: defining tables and views, writing transformations that clean and join source data, scheduling those jobs, and testing that results match expectations. Teams model data in layers, often landing raw data first, then conforming it into shared dimensions and facts, then publishing curated marts that analysts and models both consume. Feature engineering for AI is usually expressed as the same kind of SQL transformation, materialised into tables that training and scoring jobs read at consistent points in time. Version control, code review, and automated tests have become normal for warehouse code, and notebooks or SQL editors sit alongside dashboards as the interfaces people actually use. Where models are served in the platform, the work shifts toward registering the model, pointing it at a table or view, and monitoring the predictions it writes back.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Because the same storage now feeds both analysts and models, access control, row and column level policies, masking of sensitive fields, and audit logging apply to AI workloads exactly as they do to reporting. Provenance matters: teams need to know which source tables and transformations produced a given feature or prediction, and lineage tools trace that path through the layers. Data quality checks, freshness monitoring, and clear ownership of each table reduce the risk of a model quietly training on stale or duplicated records. Cost governance is part of the same picture, since compute for training and inference draws on the same budgets as queries, and untracked jobs can dominate spend. Regulations and internal policies vary by sector and jurisdiction, so the practical approach is to keep data in governed storage, document lineage, and let policy follow the data rather than copying it out.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward fewer copies and tighter coupling: models called as SQL functions, embeddings stored beside the rows they describe, and retrieval over tables handled inside the platform rather than in a separate vector store. Open table formats and catalogs are maturing so that different engines can read the same governed data, which reduces lock in and makes the lakehouse a shared substrate rather than a single vendor's product. Expect more automation around feature definitions, lineage, and quality checks, and more emphasis on measuring whether in platform models actually improve decisions rather than just being available. The open questions are practical ones: how to keep costs predictable as inference joins the query mix, and how to keep governance meaningful when the same tables serve both a dashboard and a model.
